units: the hall can be entered before sunrise
the person in charge lays the equipment out on the floor before the group turns up
those taking part leave their things beside the partition
the warm-up puts a walk together with a run
clapped hands give the jumps their beat
a ball-returning drill is done in pairs
the session closes with seated stretching
each pupil's progress is written down
text: The doors of the sports hall are unlocked before sunrise, and the wooden floor still carries a film of damp. A stocky coach lays out hoops along the centre line, then sets a row of low cones behind them. The pupils file in, drop their bags against the partition and pull on shoes with pale soles. Warming up starts with a long striding walk, arms reaching for the ceiling, and turns into an easy run around the room. Jumps follow, feet together first and then alternating, while the coach claps out the beat. After that come passes in pairs, each player returning the ball without ever holding it. At the end the group sits in a circle and works on the calves. The coach writes down what every one of them has managed, then opens the windows to air the hall before the next lot arrive.

units: the writer finds it contradictory to demand activity while doing away with open space
school play areas are losing ground
empty plots are turned over to parked cars
journeys on foot vanish in the name of road danger
young children are out of breath after one flight of stairs
the writer blames the surroundings rather than any want of will
a child who has never moved on rough ground breaks a fall badly
the fear of falling makes the stillness worse
the writer asks above all for school approaches that can be walked
text: We tell children to get moving, then we take away the places where moving is possible. That is the contradiction that irritates me. Playgrounds shrink year on year, spare ground goes over to parked cars, and getting anywhere on foot disappears because the roads are held to be dangerous. The upshot: youngsters wheezing after a single flight of stairs, tense the moment an unfamiliar effort is asked of them. This is not idleness, it is a consequence. A child who has never run over rough ground has no idea how to break a fall; he lands badly, hurts himself, and takes fright. The fright keeps him still, and round the loop goes again. So yes, add supervised sessions, but make the streets around the schools walkable first. Movement is learnt by walking, by climbing, by stumbling, not only in a slot pencilled on a timetable.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman in charge of the swimming group failed first as a competitor
her uneven stroke cost her ground at every turn
she thought about leaving the sport
a doctor traced the trouble to the set of a shoulder
the fault came of growing too fast
she spent a full season reworking her technique with film to help
her times came down once that was put right
she forbids heavy repetition while the posture is wrong
text: Long before she took charge of a group, the swimming coach at the local club failed as a competitor. As a teenager she swam length after length without improving, held back at every turn by a jerky, broken stroke. Her times stalled and she thought about leaving the water for good. It was a sports doctor who eventually spotted a badly set shoulder, the legacy of growing too fast. Rather than train harder, she gave a whole season to relearning her catch, filmed from below, adjusting the entry of the hand a fraction at a time. The stroke came out long and even, and her times fell away. She now works the same way with the swimmers she looks after: film, show, correct one thing per session. She will not allow endless sets while the position is still wrong, and her group has turned out strong over distance.

units: the writer used two different climbing places in the same season
the first one sits in an old building with little light
its holds have been rubbed smooth by use
the routes there call for balance more than for pulling
the second place is full of colour and its routes are reset every week
the second one draws out leaping, showy moves
the writer prefers the dark one without calling it better
he puts that choice down to the care he must give his feet
text: Two climbing walls took my money in the same season, and nothing about them agrees. The first sits under an old market hall and keeps the gloom of a place nobody thought worth repainting. Its holds are worn, rubbed smooth by countless palms, and the routes ask you to find your balance far more than to haul on your arms. You climb slowly there, almost without speaking, and come down with your forearms on fire. The second wall is a riot of colour: high panels, deep matting, routes stripped out and reset every week. Everything about it invites the lunge, the leap, the move worth watching. A seasoned climber will take patience from the one and pure play from the other. I prefer the dark hall, though I would not call it the better of the two: it makes me listen to my feet, where the other flatters my arms.

units: the writer sets out, as asked, the method he has kept to since taking the sport up again
he records how long each outing lasts and how fast it was
he takes his pulse on waking, lying down
he does strength work twice a week without heavy loads
he uses two pairs of shoes according to how long the outing is
he advises drinking before thirst arrives
he stops building whenever two sessions in a row feel like a burden
he credits this record-keeping with keeping fresh injuries away
text: You asked me to set out the routine I have kept to since I started again, so here it is, heading by heading. Training load: I write down every outing, the time on my feet, the average pace, how the last stretch of it felt. Recovery: I keep an eye on sleep and on my pulse when I wake, taken lying down before I get up. Strength: twice a week is quite enough, side planks, calf raises, hip extensions, never chasing a heavy load. Kit: I rotate two pairs of shoes, a light one for the short outings and a cushioned one for the longer ones. Food: nothing out of the ordinary, beyond drinking before the thirst arrives. Mood, last of all: I stop building the moment two outings in a row feel like a burden. The notebook is an ugly thing, but it keeps me upright and it has kept fresh injuries away.

units: a question is put about the youngest age for carrying a load
before schooling begins no added load is called for
the very young child works with his own weight by climbing
the stage that follows puts the quality of the movement above the resistance
a light implement and a reflection are enough at that stage
the equipment must suit the build of the child
an adult's kit must not be taken over
two short training sessions are worth more than one very long one
the exercise halts as soon as the hold of the back gives way
text: A listener puts the question of the age at which a child may lift a load without coming to harm. The answer follows a progression which ought to be kept to in order. Before school begins, no outside load serves any purpose: the child has quite enough in his own weight, which he shifts about by climbing and rolling. Then comes a stage in which learning the movement counts for more than the resistance, and a light stick with a mirror beats a loaded bar. A second question bears on equipment, which must suit the build of the child and never be taken over from an adult. A third bears on how often, and the answer holds in a line: two short, regular sessions beat one that drags on. Watchfulness comes last, and it must stay keen, for the moment the back gives way the exercise halts.

units: a young athlete reports a pain in the knee after three climbs
he had doubled the length of his outings inside a week
the coach explains that tendons come along more slowly than the lungs
the pain arises from that gap in adaptation
the young man believed he could take on more
the coach adds that the sense of ease arrives before the tissue is ready
they agree on an easier restart and a modest weekly rise
the coach weighs the cost of a neglected injury against that of a short pause
text: A teenager told his coach that a burning came into his knee as soon as he reached the third climb. The coach asked him what had changed in the way he was preparing, and the boy owned up to doubling the length of his outings inside a week. Tendons, the coach said, come along more slowly than the lungs do, and the pain sat exactly in that gap. The boy answered that he still felt able to take on more. He was told that the sense of ease arrives well before the tissue is ready, which is what catches beginners out. So the two of them agreed on an easier restart, with the build kept to a small amount each week. The boy wanted to know how long a thing like that would go on for; a hurt knee left alone costs a season, came the reply, while caution accepted costs a handful of outings.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: carriers of letters once crossed high ground with no path and no pack animal
one man on his own gave out before he reached the end
the letter was liable to come late or to be lost
the answer they found was to hand the load on
shelters were set out at even gaps
each shelter held a rested carrier who left again at once
the overall speed of carriage was doubled
the carriers stopped holding back, their own share being short
this way of cutting up an impossible effort still serves elsewhere
text: Picture messengers who had to cross whole valleys on foot, with no track cut for them and no animal to carry the load. The work broke people, and the snag was easily put: one man on his own gives out before the end, so the letter comes late or never comes at all. The answer they hit on was the handover. Shelters were set out at even gaps, each one holding a fresh runner who took the leather pouch and left again at once. The stretch to be covered in one go turned bearable, and the speed of the whole thing doubled. Better still, the runners stopped holding anything back: knowing their own share was short, they ran it flat out. And there sits an idea we still lean on, from the carriage of goods to races run by teams, which is to cut an impossible effort into portions a body can hold.

units: what tells the two runners apart is the way muscular energy is spent
the sprinter carries mostly fast-contracting fibres
those fibres are powerful but give out in moments
the distance runner carries fine, slow fibres
those fibres burn oxygen without tiring
the sprinter builds up a breathing debt that he pays back afterwards
the distance runner sets his pace so as to avoid that debt
their training differs, repeated starts against long outings
how the fibres are shared out is partly inherited
text: What sets a sprinter apart from a distance runner, if not the way in which his muscles spend the energy they hold? The first leans on fast fibres, thick ones, good for a short and violent contraction that dies away almost at once. The second carries slow fibres, finer and less brisk, which burn oxygen all day without tiring. The sprinter builds his effort with the breath more or less held, then pays the debt back afterwards, gasping. The distance runner sets a pace that never digs such a hole in the first place. The training shows it too: the one repeats his starts and takes his recoveries in full, the other piles up long outings at a held effort. Training tips the balance one way or the other without overturning it, since the share of fibres is partly a thing that you inherit.

units: the narrator recalls a walk along a soaked ridge line
the soles made a sucking noise in the mud
a stone came away down the face during the climb
the walk was led by an elderly woman at a steady pace
the others in the party climbed strung out
the top was reached all at once
a hard wind dried the clothes in an instant
they came down a gentler side and said nothing
text: On the ridge path the mud made every footfall slide, and I remember that outing better than I remember any of the others. There was the noise first of all: the suck of boots pulling free, the shortened breathing, a stone that came away and dropped down the face. There was the woman at the front, a brisk pensioner who climbed without ever altering her pace, as though the slope had nothing to do with her. There was the rest of us strung out behind, each one setting his step by his own tiredness. And there was the crest itself, come upon all at once, with a wind that dried our jackets in the space of a breath. We went down the far side, gentler, telling each other nothing. That silence was worth more than any account of it, and I carry it still whenever a climb looks too steep.
